dom.name: Business & Management
tips: Job titles map differently from company to company (a Director may be a senior manager, a division head or a board member). Ask for business cards or an org chart before the assignment.
Numbers and acronyms (KPI, ROI, YoY) come thick and fast. Keep an acronym sheet handy and check whether the speaker says the full form or the abbreviation.
In negotiations, watch the register: keep the difference between 'there's some flexibility' and 'this is our bottom line', and don't turn a hedge into a flat statement.

dom.name: Finance & Capital Markets
tips: Taiwan usually renders the Federal Reserve with its own short name, and rate moves are often counted in 'quarter points' (one quarter point = 25 bps = 0.25 percentage points).
Keep basis points, percentage points and percent apart: mixing them up is the single most common error in financial interpreting.
Agree on how figures will be read out, and prepare conversions between the Chinese units of ten thousand (wan) and hundred million (yi) and million, billion and trillion.

dom.name: Accounting & Financial Reporting
tips: Line items differ in small but important ways (operating income vs. net income, revenue vs. sales). Render the level of the statement the speaker actually means.
Ratio terms such as gross margin must keep the 'rate' element in Chinese; never let an amount and a percentage blur together.
Listed companies in Taiwan report under IFRS; the formal name of the income statement is the 'statement of comprehensive income', though people usually just say income statement.

Supplier, vendor and contract manufacturer carry different weight in context. If the client has a preferred term, use it.

tips: Chip vocabulary differs sharply between Taiwan and mainland China (chip, process, lithography all have different words). Use Taiwanese terms in Taiwan, but be ready to recognize the mainland versions from PRC speakers.

dom.name: Manufacturing & Industry
tips: Manufacturing assignments often happen on the factory floor. Learn the equipment, process and safety vocabulary first, and ask for a walk-through of the line if you can.
Yield, defect rate and utilization move in opposite directions (higher is better for some, lower for others). Render the figure and its direction together.
Shop-floor jargon and acronyms (SOP, WIP, BOM) are everywhere. When in doubt, ask the speaker to repeat: one wrong word can affect a whole work order.

dom.name: Energy & Environment
tips: Energy and environment are politically charged topics (nuclear power, carbon fees). Stay neutral and convey figures and positions faithfully.
Keep capacity (kW, MW, GW) and energy (kWh, MWh, GWh) apart, and never drop the "e" in tonnes of CO2e.
Water shortages, the operating reserve margin and environmental impact assessments are Taiwan-specific topics with established terms: use them rather than coining your own.

dom.name: Law
tips: Common-law concepts don't always map onto Taiwan's civil-law system (plea bargaining, case law). Where there is no equivalent, keep the original term and explain it briefly.
Court interpreters in Taiwan must be faithful and complete, adding and omitting nothing; don't smooth out the speaker's legal wording.
Judgments, rulings and orders are different instruments and must not be mixed up; hearing also varies with the type of proceeding.
